extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, judges, and practitioners (and advanced law students) interested in remedial doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and doctrinal criteria for deciding remedial outcomes in judicial review of agency action—when to vacate, remand (with or without vacatur), or treat an agency error as harmless. Focuses on court-side balancing tests, circuit variations, and statutory cues in the APA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of prejudicial error / holding agency interpretations to stand
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency has adopted a reasonable construction of a statute, indicates a preference for that interpretation over alternatives, and represents to a reviewing court that it would stick to that interpretation even if the statute could be read differently, the rule of prejudicial error suggests that the interpretation should stand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a basis for leaving agency interpretations intact where the agency would likely reinstate the same position on remand; functions as an argument for treating some Prill/Chenery-type problems as non-prejudicial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmless error doctrine in administrative review
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal courts sometimes uphold unsound agency decisions when they are confident the agency would reach the same decision on remand—i.e., the agency error is harmless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequently applied in immigration and social security disability contexts where the record indicates the claimant could not prevail; courts sometimes label such harmlessness as an 'exception to the Chenery doctrine.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmlessness because error is de minimis / peripheral factual mistake
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency error may be held harmless when it consists of a factual mistake of peripheral significance that had no bearing on the substance of the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include minor factual inaccuracies that are de minimis (e.g., PDK Labs v. DEA; Curry v. Sullivan). Courts treat such mistakes as irrelevant to the ultimate outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmlessness because the record overwhelmingly supports the result
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency error may be held harmless even if the error is serious, provided the evidence in the record so strongly supports the result that the court is confident the agency would reach the same decision on remand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative cases: In re Watts (Fed. Cir.), Nazaraghaie (10th Cir.). This ground is controversial but commonly invoked where the administrative record makes a different outcome highly unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge Friendly / Massachusetts Trustees standard (significant chance test)
rubrics_metrics.description: A remand is necessary only when the reviewing court concludes that there is a significant chance that, but for the error, the agency might have reached a different decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterizes a permissive approach to harmlessness and remand; the excerpt cites Judge Friendly endorsing this view as a sensible indentation of Chenery (Mass. Trs.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Circuit standard for harmless error (tangential or overwhelming evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: An error cannot be harmless unless it is tangential to the result or overwhelming evidence supporting the administrative adjudicator’s findings makes it clear that the same decision would have been reached in the absence of the errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authority: Cao He Lin v. U.S. Dep’t of Justice. Courts applying this standard require either irrelevance or record strength amounting to certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: D.C., Seventh, and Ninth Circuit variants (confidence / predictability formulations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Various circuits articulate harmlessness in formulations like: affirm only when 'there is not the slightest uncertainty as to the outcome' (D.C. Cir.), when it is 'predictable with great confidence' the agency will reinstate the decision (7th Cir.), or in disability cases only if the court can 'confidently conclude that no reasonable ALJ... could have reached a different disability determination' (9th Cir.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These formulations are functionally similar but differ in stringency and contexts of application (e.g., disability, rulemaking).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allied-Signal remand-without-vacatur factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision whether to vacate depends on (1) the seriousness of the order's deficiencies (and thus the extent of doubt whether the agency chose correctly) and (2) the disruptive consequences of an interim change that may itself be changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This two-part test (from Allied-Signal) is the D.C. Circuit's touchstone for remanding without vacating agency rules; courts weigh deficiency seriousness against practical disruption of vacatur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory text cues from APA §706 (set aside vs take due account)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although APA §706(2)(A) directs courts to 'set aside' arbitrary or capricious agency actions, the APA also instructs that 'due account shall be taken of prejudicial error,' authorizing courts to hold agency errors harmless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This textual reading supports the argument that the APA permits remedial flexibility (holding errors harmless) akin to harmless-error doctrines in other judicial contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical-consequences concern about remand without vacatur
rubrics_metrics.description: Remanding without vacating may leave agencies with little incentive to correct errors; agencies often delay or ignore remand orders, sometimes prompting courts to issue writs of mandamus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical observation and citations (Daugirdas) document agency dilatoriness; courts and commentators express concern that remand-only dispositions can function as indefinite stays and reduce remedial bite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situations where remand without vacatur may be appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Remand without vacatur may be appropriate when (a) asking the agency to clarify an issue that may recur, (b) there is reason to think the agency might reconsider, or (c) leaving the rule intact temporarily preserves important substantive values (e.g., environmental protections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: North Carolina v. EPA (preserving environmental values), using withholding of the mandate for a fixed period, or remanding when proregulatory groups prefer a rule to none at all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial tradeoffs assessment (costs of vacatur vs systemic benefits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should weigh whether the costs of vacating flawed agency action (disruption, resource drain, potential harm) outweigh the systemic benefits of insisting on robust reason-giving and agency accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include agency resource constraints, consequences for mass adjudication, whether vacating would improve agency decisionmaking quality, and whether forcing reexplanation creates 'make-work' with little public benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for deliberate guardrails and doctrinal guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Because lower courts apply harmless-error and remand-without-vacatur inconsistently, there is a need for more deliberate standards or guardrails to reconcile Chenery's formalism with harmlessness-based discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should supply clearer analytical frameworks (e.g., contingent standards based on diligence, interest at stake, type of error) rather than haphazard practice; commentators offer context-dependent approaches (e.g., Hemel & Nielson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Supreme Court precedents on remedial doctrine (limits and signals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supreme Court decisions (e.g., Perez v. Mortgage Bankers Ass’n; Michigan v. EPA; Shinseki v. Sanders) both constrain doctrinal innovations and provide interpretive signals about when remand-without-vacatur or harmlessness may be permissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perez criticized D.C. Circuit innovations that conflicted with the APA's 'clear text' (suggesting courts should be cautious about novel remedial doctrines); Kagan's Chevron-based dissent in Michigan suggests Chevron-style defenses can support harmlessness reasoning; Sanders reiterates harmless-error principles.
